sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Dumbbell Row is a compound pulling exercise that targets the back muscles by rowing two dumbbells from a hinged position.

Performed with a forward hip hinge and an overhand grip, this movement builds thickness and strength across the lats, rhomboids, and traps while also engaging the biceps and core.

Dumbbells allow each arm to work independently, helping to identify and correct strength imbalances between sides.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Builds a thick, strong back across the lats, rhomboids, and traps
- Each arm works independently to correct muscle imbalances
- The hip hinge position isometrically strengthens the posterior chain
- Improves posture by strengthening the upper back and rear shoulders
- Greater range of motion compared to barbell rows
- Engages the core throughout as a stabiliser
- Versatile — can be performed standing, on a bench, or with various grips

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Back (Latissimus Dorsi, Rhomboids, Trapezius)

Secondary: Biceps, Rear Deltoids, Erector Spinae, Core (Rectus Abdominis, Obliques), Forearms and Grip

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Hold two dumbbells in front of your body with an overhand grip.
3. Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor.
4. Keep your back straight and your core braced.
5. Let the dumbbells hang at arm's length toward the ground.
6. Maintain a slight bend in your knees for stability.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding two dumbbells in front of your body with an overhand grip.
2. Hinge forward at the hips, keeping your back straight and the dumbbells hanging toward the ground.
3. Pull the dumbbells up toward your ribcage, keeping your elbows close to your sides and squeezing your shoulder blades toward your spine.
4. Slowly lower the dumbbells back down to the starting position, keeping control of the weight throughout the movement, and repeat for the desired number of reps.
5. Focus on initiating the pull with your back muscles, not your biceps.
6. Pause briefly at the top of each rep to maximise the contraction.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Using momentum to swing the dumbbells up instead of rowing with control
- Rounding the lower back during the hip hinge
- Flaring the elbows wide instead of keeping them close to the body
- Standing too upright, reducing the range of motion
- Not squeezing the shoulder blades together at the top
- Letting the dumbbells drop quickly on the way down
- Using uneven pulling — one arm doing more work than the other

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Two dumbbells of equal weight
- Flat, stable surface to stand on
- Optional: Chalk for grip assistance
- Optional: Lifting straps for heavier loads
- Optional: Flat bench for single-arm supported variation
- Recommended: Start with a moderate weight to master the hinge and row pattern

sections.heading: Choosing Your Dumbbell Weight
sections.content:
1. Beginners: Start with 5-10 kg per hand (men) or 2-5 kg per hand (women).
2. Intermediate: 12-25 kg per hand (men) or 6-12 kg per hand (women).
3. The weight should challenge your back without causing your lower back to round.
4. If you cannot maintain a flat back in the hinge, reduce the weight.
5. You should be able to pause at the top of each row with control.
6. Progress gradually as your back strength and hip hinge endurance improve.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Feet: Shoulder-width apart, firmly planted.
2. Knees: Slight bend, maintained throughout.
3. Hips: Hinged back, torso at roughly 45 degrees.
4. Spine: Flat and neutral from head to tailbone.
5. Shoulders: Pulled back and down, away from the ears.
6. Arms: Fully extended at the bottom, elbows driving back at the top.
7. Head: Neutral, eyes looking a few feet ahead on the floor.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Barbell Bent Over Row: Heavier bilateral rowing with a barbell
- Kettlebell Row: Similar movement pattern with kettlebells
- Single Arm Dumbbell Row: Unilateral version with bench support
- T-Bar Row: Machine-supported rowing for back thickness
- Cable Row: Seated cable pulling for constant tension
- Inverted Row: Bodyweight pulling exercise for beginners

sections.heading: Dumbbell Row Variations
sections.content:
Standing Dumbbell Row: Standard bilateral bent-over row with two dumbbells
Single Arm Dumbbell Row: One arm at a time with bench support
Incline Bench Dumbbell Row: Chest supported on incline bench to isolate the back
Renegade Row: Rowing from a push up position for core challenge
Underhand Dumbbell Row: Supinated grip for more bicep involvement
Slow Tempo Dumbbell Row: 3-4 second eccentric for time under tension

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Pain: Use a chest-supported incline bench row to remove spinal loading
Grip Fatigue: Use chalk or lifting straps for heavier sets
Shoulder Issues: Keep elbows tight to the body and try an underhand grip
Hamstring Tightness: Bend the knees slightly more to reduce strain in the hinge
Core Weakness: Use a lighter weight and focus on bracing throughout
Learning Stage: Start with single arm rows using a bench for support before progressing to the standing bilateral version
